implementation_notes: Every Java object is a monitor, so the classic structure is language semantics rather than a library: wait() releases the intrinsic lock and parks the thread in the object's wait set, notifyAll() wakes all of them and each re-acquires the lock before returning. Oracle's Guarded Blocks tutorial requires the wait to sit inside a loop that tests the predicate and notes that a notification does not prove this thread's condition holds; notifyAll is the safe default and notify is only for a large pool of interchangeable waiters. Move to j.u.c Condition when one lock must serve several distinct wait sets, and to BlockingQueue when the guard is literally 'an item is available'.
pitfalls: Swallowing InterruptedException (or clearing the interrupt without rethrowing) breaks cancellation and shutdown for the whole wait set.
Calling wait/notify outside synchronized throws IllegalMonitorStateException, and calling wait while holding a second lock invites deadlock.
notify() wakes an arbitrary waiter: with two predicates on one monitor it can wake a thread whose guard is still false while the thread that could proceed stays parked.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition (multiple wait sets)
variants.implementation_notes: Condition factors the Object monitor methods out into distinct wait sets per lock, which removes the wake-the-wrong-waiter problem of a bounded buffer: one condition for not-empty and one for not-full, each signalled only when its own predicate changes; await atomically releases the associated lock and always returns holding it again, and the JDK documents that spurious wake-ups are permitted so the predicate loop stays mandatory. Choose it over intrinsic monitors when a single lock serves several predicates or when timed/uninterruptible waits are needed.
pitfalls: A Condition is intrinsically bound to the lock that created it, and the JDK recommends never using one as a monitor object as well.
signal still permits spurious wake-ups, so the predicate must be re-checked even with a private wait set.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue take/put (library guard)
variants.implementation_notes: BlockingQueue packages guarded suspension as a type: take() waits for the queue to become non-empty and put() waits for space, in blocking, timed and interruptible forms, with the happens-before edge documented; the JDK shows the producer-consumer usage and warns that close or shutdown is not intrinsic, so termination needs an end-of-stream marker such as a poison pill. Prefer it whenever the guard is 'items or space available', and keep the monitor or Condition forms for guards that are not queue-shaped.
pitfalls: BlockingQueue has no close/shutdown operation, so a missing poison pill leaves consumers parked forever.
put() on a full queue blocks the producer: choose a capacity and use offer(timeout) where a stalled producer is a liveness risk.
